gloss: A physical activity played by rules for competition or fun.
examples: Soccer is the only *sport* he really follows.
The school offers a dozen different *sports* in the fall.
Swimming is a good *sport* for people with bad knees.
contrast: Americans say *sports* where the British say *sport*: he plays sports vs. he plays sport.

gloss: A contest played by set rules, or one single contest in a series.
examples: We won the *game* by three points.
There are two *games* left in the season.
Chess is a *game* of patience.

gloss: A single contest between two players or two teams.
examples: The tennis *match* went on for four hours.
Both *matches* got rained out.
He lost the *match* in straight sets.

gloss: The game played on a large field by two sides of eleven who move the ball mostly with their feet.
examples: My daughter plays *soccer* on Saturdays.
*Soccer* is finally getting decent TV ratings here.
He coached youth *soccer* for ten years.
contrast: *Soccer* is the American name for the game the rest of the world calls football.

ru: американский футбол; мяч для этой игры
countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The American game played with an oval ball and helmets, or the ball used in it.
examples: He played *football* in high school.
Somebody left two *footballs* out in the rain.
*Football* season starts in September.
contrast: In the US *football* means American football; the game played with the feet is *soccer*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The indoor game in which two teams of five throw a ball through a raised hoop, or the ball itself.
examples: She has a full ride for *basketball*.
The gym had a bin of worn-out *basketballs*.
We watched college *basketball* all weekend.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The American game played with a bat and a small hard ball, or that ball.
examples: *Baseball* is still my dad's favorite sport.
He keeps a shelf of signed *baseballs*.
We have *baseball* tickets for Friday.

gloss: A fast game played on ice in which players hit a rubber disk into the other team's goal.
examples: He's played *hockey* since he was five.
*Hockey* is huge in Minnesota.
They watch *hockey* every Saturday night.

gloss: A game in which two or four players hit a ball over a net with rackets.
examples: Do you want to play *tennis* on Sunday?
She took up *tennis* after she retired.
*Tennis* is easier on your knees than running.

gloss: A game in which players hit a small ball into a series of holes with clubs.
examples: My boss talks about *golf* nonstop.
He plays *golf* every Saturday morning.
*Golf* eats up an entire afternoon.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A game in which two teams hit a ball back and forth over a high net, or the ball used.
examples: We played beach *volleyball* until it got dark.
The equipment closet is full of flat *volleyballs*.
She got a scholarship for *volleyball*.

gloss: The sport of fighting with padded gloves inside a roped ring.
examples: He took up *boxing* to get in shape.
*Boxing* isn't as popular as it used to be.
There's a *boxing* gym two blocks from here.

gloss: The sport of gripping an opponent and trying to pin him to the mat.
examples: *Wrestling* practice starts at six in the morning.
She got into *wrestling* in middle school.
College *wrestling* has strict weight classes.
contrast: The *w* is silent: RES-ling.

gloss: The activity or sport of moving through water with your arms and legs.
examples: *Swimming* is the best workout for your back.
She quit *swimming* after high school.
There's no *swimming* allowed after dark.

gloss: The activity or sport of moving fast on foot for exercise or in a race.
examples: *Running* wrecked my knees.
He got into *running* after he turned forty.
*Running* on a treadmill bores me to death.

gloss: The sport or activity of riding a bicycle.
examples: *Cycling* is big in this part of the state.
She switched from running to *cycling*.
Indoor *cycling* classes fill up fast.

gloss: The sport of moving over snow on long narrow boards attached to your boots.
examples: We go *skiing* every February.
*Skiing* out west is a whole different thing.
He gave up *skiing* after he broke his leg.
contrast: Keep both i's: ski + -ing spells *skiing*, and it is two syllables, SKEE-ing.

gloss: The activity of moving on ice or pavement wearing skates.
examples: The pond is finally hard enough for *skating*.
Figure *skating* takes years of lessons.
There's public *skating* every Friday night.

gloss: The sport of riding ocean waves standing on a board.
examples: He drove down the coast for the *surfing*.
*Surfing* looks easy until you try it.
The *surfing* is best early in the morning.

gloss: The sport of going up rock or walls using your hands and feet.
examples: Indoor *climbing* got her over her fear of heights.
He's into rock *climbing* now.
*Climbing* is harder on your fingers than you'd think.
contrast: The *b* is silent: KLY-ming, not KLIMB-ing.

gloss: The game of rolling a heavy ball down a lane to knock over pins.
examples: *Bowling* is the only sport my whole family will do.
There's a *bowling* alley by the mall.
We went *bowling* for his birthday.

gloss: The sport of jumping headfirst into water, or of swimming underwater with tanks.
examples: She won a medal in *diving*.
Scuba *diving* is expensive to get into.
The pool is too shallow for *diving*.

gloss: A system of stretches, poses, and breathing done for fitness and calm.
examples: *Yoga* fixed my lower back.
She teaches *yoga* on Tuesday nights.
I do twenty minutes of *yoga* before work.

gloss: A Japanese martial art of fighting with sharp blows of the hands and feet.
examples: Both kids take *karate* after school.
He has a black belt in *karate*.
*Karate* taught her more discipline than anything else.
contrast: The final *e* is pronounced: kuh-RAH-tee, not kuh-RAHT.

gloss: A board game for two players using sixteen pieces each on a checkered board.
examples: My grandfather taught me *chess*.
He plays *chess* online every night.
*Chess* is having a real moment right now.

gloss: A rough team game played with an oval ball that players carry, kick, and pass backward.
examples: He played *rugby* in college.
*Rugby* never really caught on here.
There's a *rugby* club that practices in the park.

gloss: A running race of just over twenty-six miles.
examples: She finished her first *marathon* in four hours.
He's run six *marathons* since he turned fifty.
Training for a *marathon* takes about four months.

gloss: Someone who takes part in a game or sport.
examples: He's the best *player* on the team.
Two *players* got hurt in the first half.
She's a solid *player*, just not a star.

gloss: The official who enforces the rules during a game.
examples: The *referee* called a foul on the play.
Both *referees* missed it.
Nobody wants to be a *referee* in youth soccer.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable: ref-uh-REE.

gloss: The official who calls plays in baseball, tennis, and some other sports.
examples: The *umpire* threw him out of the game.
Both *umpires* agreed the ball was foul.
He argued with the *umpire* for ten minutes.

gloss: The person or team that finishes first in a competition.
examples: She's the defending *champion*.
The *champions* got a parade downtown.
He was a state wrestling *champion* in high school.

gloss: The person or team you are playing against.
examples: His *opponent* was a foot taller.
They studied film on their next three *opponents*.
Never underestimate an *opponent* you don't know.

gloss: A team or person you compete against again and again.
examples: We play our biggest *rival* on Friday.
The two *rivals* have met in the final four times.
He beat his old *rival* in three sets.

gloss: Someone who follows and supports a team, player, or sport.
examples: I've been a *fan* since I was a kid.
Thousands of *fans* showed up in the rain.
He's a huge hockey *fan*.

gloss: Someone who watches an event without taking part.
examples: *Spectators* had to stay behind the fence.
One *spectator* ran onto the field.
It's a great *spectator* sport.
contrast: Americans stress the first syllable, SPEK-tay-tur; the British say spek-TAY-tuh.

gloss: The player whose job is to keep the ball or puck out of the goal.
examples: Their *goalie* stopped forty shots.
Both *goalies* played the whole game.
He's been a *goalie* since he was eight.

gloss: The baseball player who throws the ball to the batter.
examples: Their starting *pitcher* left in the fifth inning.
They went through four *pitchers* in one game.
He was a *pitcher* in high school.
contrast: Don't confuse it with *picture* (PIK-chur) — *pitcher* has no k sound.

gloss: The football player who directs the attack and throws most of the passes.
examples: Their *quarterback* threw three touchdowns.
Two *quarterbacks* went down with injuries.
He's the best *quarterback* they've had in years.

gloss: Someone who fights in the sport of boxing.
examples: The *boxer* went down in the third round.
Both *boxers* made weight.
He trains amateur *boxers* on weekends.

gloss: Someone who swims, especially in competition.
examples: She's the fastest *swimmer* on the team.
The *swimmers* were in the pool by five.
He's a strong *swimmer* but a terrible runner.

gloss: Someone who guides a person's training or treats athletes' injuries.
examples: She hired a personal *trainer* in January.
The *trainer* taped his ankle at halftime.
Both *trainers* work with the football team.
contrast: In Britain *trainers* also means sneakers; in the US it only means a person.

gloss: A player in his or her first season on a professional team.
examples: The *rookie* scored twenty points in his first start.
Three *rookies* made the roster.
For a *rookie*, she's incredibly calm.

gloss: Someone who plays on the same team as you.
examples: His *teammates* carried him off the field.
She's a good *teammate* even when she isn't playing.
Two former *teammates* now coach against each other.

gloss: The team or player everyone expects to lose.
examples: Nobody minds rooting for the *underdog*.
They went in as ten-point *underdogs* and won.
She's the *underdog* in every match she plays.

gloss: Someone who runs, especially as a sport.
examples: He's a long-distance *runner*.
Thousands of *runners* lined up at the start.
She's the fastest *runner* in her grade.

gloss: A racket game played over a high net with a light feathered shuttlecock.
examples: We played *badminton* in the backyard all summer.
*Badminton* looks easy until you try to return a smash.
The gym has *badminton* courts on Tuesday nights.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A game like baseball played with a larger, softer ball, or that ball itself.
examples: She pitched for her high school *softball* team.
He hit the *softball* over the fence.
The company league plays *softball* on Thursdays.

gloss: A team game in which players carry a small ball in a netted stick.
examples: *Lacrosse* is huge at colleges on the East Coast.
My brother plays *lacrosse* in the spring.
She got a scholarship for *lacrosse*.

gloss: The sport of shooting arrows at a target with a bow.
examples: Summer camp offered swimming, canoeing, and *archery*.
He took up *archery* after he hurt his knee.
*Archery* takes more patience than strength.

gloss: The sport of fighting with thin swords under strict rules.
examples: She started *fencing* in middle school.
*Fencing* is one of the oldest Olympic sports.
The club teaches *fencing* twice a week.
contrast: The same word also means the fences around a yard: a hundred feet of fencing.

gloss: The activity of riding and doing tricks on a skateboard.
examples: *Skateboarding* is banned in front of the courthouse.
He broke his wrist *skateboarding*.
The city built a park for *skateboarding* and BMX.

gloss: The activity or sport of traveling in a boat driven by the wind.
examples: They go *sailing* on the lake every weekend.
*Sailing* is harder than it looks in a crosswind.
He learned *sailing* from his grandfather.

gloss: The sport of moving a boat with oars, usually as a crew.
examples: *Rowing* practice starts at five in the morning.
She got into college partly because of *rowing*.
*Rowing* works almost every muscle you have.

gloss: Running at a slow, steady pace for exercise.
examples: He does twenty minutes of *jogging* before work.
*Jogging* on pavement is hard on the knees.
She met her husband *jogging* around the reservoir.

gloss: The sport or activity of lifting heavy barbells.
examples: *Weightlifting* has three lifts at the Olympics.
He gave up running for *weightlifting*.
The team does *weightlifting* twice a week in the off-season.

gloss: A fighting sport such as karate or judo, practiced under a system of rules.
examples: Judo is the only *martial art* he has ever studied.
The kids take *martial arts* on Saturday mornings.
She teaches a *martial art* that came from Brazil.
contrast: Watch the letters: *martial* (fighting) is not *marital* (about marriage).

gloss: A game played on a table with small paddles and a light hollow ball.
examples: There's a *table tennis* table in the break room.
*Table tennis* became an Olympic sport in 1988.
He was the state champion in *table tennis*.
contrast: Americans usually call the casual version ping-pong and save table tennis for the real sport.

gloss: The sport that covers running, jumping, and throwing events.
examples: She ran *track and field* all four years of high school.
*Track and field* is the heart of the Summer Olympics.
The school cut *track and field* to save money.
contrast: Americans say *track and field*; the British call the same sport athletics.

gloss: A race combining swimming, cycling, and running in one event.
examples: He finished his first *triathlon* last June.
Two of the *triathlons* were canceled for bad weather.
Training for a *triathlon* takes over your whole summer.

gloss: A card game in which players bet on the value of the hand they hold.
examples: They play *poker* in the garage on Friday nights.
He lost eighty dollars at *poker*.
*Poker* is as much about reading people as about cards.

gloss: A game played by moving pieces on a marked board.
examples: Monopoly was the only *board game* we owned.
The shelf is full of *board games* nobody plays.
A *board game* is a good way to get through a rainy day.

gloss: A game or problem that tests your cleverness or patience.
examples: She does the crossword *puzzle* every morning.
The kids finished a thousand-piece *puzzle* over break.
Logic *puzzles* are on the back page.

gloss: The small numbered cubes thrown to decide moves in a game.
examples: Roll the *dice* and move your piece.
One of the *dice* fell under the couch.
The game comes with two *dice* and a spinner.
contrast: *Dice* works as both singular and plural in everyday speech; the old singular *die* survives mainly in the saying the die is cast.

gloss: A game played on a screen with a console, computer, or phone.
examples: He got a *video game* for his birthday.
*Video games* keep him up half the night.
This *video game* is rated for teens.

gloss: Someone who plays video games seriously or often.
examples: My roommate is a serious *gamer*.
Thousands of *gamers* watched the tournament online.
She's a casual *gamer* — an hour on Sundays.

gloss: The move in chess that traps the king and ends the game.
examples: He saw *checkmate* four moves ahead.
It was *checkmate* in under twenty minutes.
She forced *checkmate* with a rook and a bishop.

gloss: The smallest and most numerous chess piece.
examples: He opened by pushing a *pawn* two squares.
She traded a *pawn* for a better position.
You start with eight *pawns* across the second row.
contrast: The same spelling and sound also mean an item left at a pawn shop.

gloss: A children's game where one player looks for the others, who hide.
examples: The kids played *hide-and-seek* until dark.
*Hide-and-seek* is no fun in an empty apartment.
He's too good at *hide-and-seek* for a four-year-old.

gloss: The stringed frame with a handle used to hit a ball in tennis and similar games.
examples: He restrung his *racket* before the match.
Two of her *rackets* cracked in one season.
You can rent a *racket* at the front desk.
contrast: Also spelled *racquet*; the same word means a loud noise or a criminal scheme.

gloss: The hard rubber disk used instead of a ball in ice hockey.
examples: The *puck* went into the crowd.
He kept his eye on the *puck* the whole shift.
They lost three *pucks* over the boards.

gloss: The mesh stretched across a court or hung in a goal.
examples: Her serve caught the top of the *net*.
The ball hit the back of the *net*.
Both *nets* need to be replaced.

gloss: The small peg that holds a golf ball up for the first shot on a hole.
examples: He set the ball on the *tee*.
I keep a handful of *tees* in my bag.
Her drive knocked the *tee* ten feet away.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *tea* and like the letter T.

gloss: A boot with a blade or wheels for gliding over ice or pavement.
examples: One *skate* was a size too small.
He laced up his *skates* at the edge of the rink.
You can rent *skates* for five dollars.

gloss: One of the pair of long runners strapped to boots for sliding over snow.
examples: A *ski* came loose halfway down the hill.
His *skis* are still in the garage.
She waxed both *skis* the night before.
contrast: Spelled with one i, but the -ing form keeps two: *skiing*.

gloss: The single wide board ridden sideways down a snowy slope.
examples: He rented a *snowboard* for the weekend.
Her *snowboard* is shorter than mine.
They strapped the *snowboards* to the roof.

gloss: One of the studs on the bottom of a sports shoe, or the shoes themselves.
examples: A *cleat* tore off in the mud.
Don't wear your *cleats* in the house.
He outgrew last year's *cleats* by August.
contrast: In the plural, *cleats* usually means the shoes themselves, not just the studs.

gloss: The large board that shows the score and time of a game.
examples: Nobody looked at the *scoreboard* until the last minute.
The new *scoreboard* cost half a million dollars.
Both *scoreboards* went dark during the storm.

gloss: One of the upright posts that mark the edge of a goal.
examples: The kick hit the *goalpost* and bounced out.
Fans tore down the *goalposts* after the win.
He painted the *goalpost* white again.
contrast: In the idiom *move the goalposts*, it means changing the rules partway through.

gloss: The heavy hanging bag a boxer hits for practice.
examples: He works the *punching bag* for twenty minutes.
There are two *punching bags* in the corner of the gym.
I'm nobody's *punching bag*.
contrast: Americans say *punching bag*; the British say punchbag or punchball.

gloss: One of the light barriers a runner jumps over in a race.
examples: She clipped the last *hurdle* and still won.
He runs the four hundred meter *hurdles*.
Setting up the *hurdles* takes ten minutes.
contrast: Don't confuse it with *hurtle*, which means to rush along fast.

gloss: An enclosed sheet of ice or smooth floor for skating and hockey.
examples: The *rink* opens at noon on Saturdays.
Both *rinks* were booked for the tournament.
He drove her to the *rink* every morning at five.

gloss: A stadium built for baseball.
examples: The old *ballpark* holds forty thousand people.
We've been to six *ballparks* this summer.
Hot dogs taste better at the *ballpark*.
contrast: Also in the idiom *ballpark figure* — a rough estimate.

gloss: The low covered bench where a baseball team sits during a game.
examples: The manager came out of the *dugout* to argue.
Both *dugouts* emptied after the pitch.
He watched the ninth inning from the *dugout*.

gloss: The line marking the long edge of a field, and the area just outside it.
examples: He stepped over the *sideline* before the catch.
The coaches paced the *sidelines* all night.
Reporters wait on the *sideline* for the halftime interview.
contrast: In the idiom *on the sidelines*, it means watching instead of taking part.

gloss: The plain tiered benches where spectators sit at a game.
examples: We sat in the *bleachers* behind first base.
The *bleachers* were packed by kickoff.
Aluminum *bleachers* get brutally hot in July.
contrast: Used only in the plural; a single *bleacher* is almost never said.

gloss: The scoring area at each end of a football field.
examples: He caught the pass in the *end zone*.
Both *end zones* were painted with the team logo.
She watched him dance in the *end zone* on replay.

gloss: The raised circle of dirt a baseball pitcher throws from.
examples: The pitcher walked slowly to the *mound*.
He's been on the *mound* for six innings.
The groundskeepers rebuild the *mound* every spring.

gloss: The large grassy area of a baseball field beyond the bases.
examples: The ball dropped in shallow *outfield*.
He played *outfield* in high school.
Some *outfields* are much deeper than others.

gloss: The area where relief pitchers warm up during a baseball game.
examples: Two pitchers were warming up in the *bullpen*.
Their *bullpen* has been shaky all season.
Both *bullpens* are down the left field line.

gloss: The player whose job is to stop shots from entering the goal.
examples: Their *goalkeeper* saved two penalty kicks.
Both *goalkeepers* were sixteen years old.
She plays *goalkeeper* for the college team.
contrast: Americans usually shorten it to *goalie*, especially in hockey.

gloss: The forward whose main job is to score goals in soccer.
examples: Their *striker* scored twice in the first half.
The club paid a fortune for two *strikers*.
He was a *striker* until his knee gave out.

gloss: A player whose job is to stop the other team from scoring.
examples: The *defender* cleared the ball off the line.
Three *defenders* closed in on him at once.
She's the best *defender* on the roster.

gloss: A soccer player who plays between the defenders and the forwards.
examples: Their *midfielder* ran nine miles in the game.
The coach subbed in two fresh *midfielders*.
He's a *midfielder* who can also defend.

gloss: The baseball player who crouches behind home plate to receive pitches.
examples: The *catcher* signaled for a fastball.
Good *catchers* are hard to find.
He wore out his knees playing *catcher*.

gloss: A defensive football player who lines up just behind the linemen.
examples: The *linebacker* stopped him for no gain.
Their *linebackers* are the heart of the defense.
He's built like a *linebacker*.

gloss: The rider who races a horse professionally.
examples: The *jockey* weighed in at a hundred and twelve pounds.
Two *jockeys* were suspended after the race.
She's the first *jockey* in her family.

gloss: Someone who competes in wrestling.
examples: He was a state champion *wrestler*.
The *wrestlers* cut weight all week.
Her son wants to be a *wrestler*.
contrast: The w is silent and the t is not pronounced: RES-lur.

gloss: An athlete who competes in gymnastics.
examples: She trained as a *gymnast* from the age of four.
The *gymnasts* warmed up on the floor mat.
He's too tall to be a competitive *gymnast*.
contrast: The g is soft, as in *gym*: JIM-nast.

gloss: Someone who skis, for sport or for fun.
examples: A *skier* went off the trail in the fog.
The lift was full of *skiers* and snowboarders.
He's a better *skier* than he lets on.
contrast: Two syllables, SKEE-ur — the first part sounds like *see*, not like *sky*.

gloss: Someone who skates on ice, on wheels, or on a skateboard.
examples: The *skater* landed the jump cleanly.
A dozen *skaters* were circling the rink.
He's been a *skater* since he was six.

gloss: Someone who plays golf.
examples: My uncle is a serious *golfer*.
Four *golfers* were waiting at the first tee.
She's the best *golfer* at the club.

gloss: A competitor with a real chance of winning a title.
examples: He was a *contender* for the heavyweight belt.
Only three *contenders* are left in the division.
Nobody saw them as a *contender* in March.

gloss: An athlete who wins a medal in a competition.
examples: She's a two-time Olympic *medalist*.
All three *medalists* were under twenty-one.
The gold *medalist* skipped the press conference.
contrast: American English spells it with one l; the British write medallist.

gloss: Someone who leads the crowd in cheers and routines at a game.
examples: She was a *cheerleader* in high school.
The *cheerleaders* came out at halftime.
He's the team's biggest *cheerleader* off the field.

gloss: The costumed animal or figure that represents a team.
examples: Their *mascot* is a giant blue bird.
Two *mascots* raced around the field between innings.
The school voted to change its *mascot*.

gloss: The list of players a team starts a game with.
examples: He's batting third in the *lineup*.
The coach posted both *lineups* an hour before the game.
Her name was left off the *lineup* again.
contrast: One word as a noun; the verb is two words: the players *line up*.

gloss: The full list of players who belong to a team.
examples: There are twelve names on the *roster*.
Both *rosters* were cut down last week.
He made the *roster* as a walk-on.

gloss: The six-point score in football, made by carrying or catching the ball in the end zone.
examples: He ran forty yards for a *touchdown*.
They scored three *touchdowns* in the fourth quarter.
That *touchdown* won the game.

gloss: A baseball hit that lets the batter run all the bases and score.
examples: He hit a *home run* in his first at-bat.
She's led the league in *home runs* twice.
That *home run* cleared the scoreboard.

ru: филд-гол, гол с поля (в амер. футболе)
gloss: A three-point kick between the goalposts in football.
examples: The kicker missed a short *field goal*.
They won on a *field goal* as time expired.
He's made every one of his *field goals* this year.

gloss: An unguarded shot in basketball, given after a foul.
examples: He sank the *free throw* to tie the game.
She shoots ninety percent from the *free throw* line.
They missed eleven *free throws* and still won.

gloss: An easy basketball shot made close to the basket off the backboard.
examples: He blew an open *layup*.
The drill is nothing but *layups* for ten minutes.
She finished with a soft *layup* off the glass.

gloss: A basketball shot pushed straight down through the hoop from above.
examples: That *dunk* brought the whole gym to its feet.
He had four *dunks* in the first half.
Her *dunk* made the highlight reel.

gloss: A basketball grabbed after a missed shot bounces off the rim or board.
examples: He grabbed the *rebound* with one hand.
She had twelve points and nine *rebounds*.
They lost the game on the *rebound* battle.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, REE-bownd; the verb is rih-BOWND.

gloss: A pass that leads directly to a teammate's score.
examples: That was a beautiful *assist*.
He finished the night with ten *assists*.
She leads the team in *assists* per game.

gloss: A move against the rules of a game, usually punished by the referee.
examples: The referee called a *foul* on the play.
He picked up his fifth *foul* and sat down.
Two *fouls* in a row cost them the lead.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *fowl*, meaning a bird.

gloss: One of the nine parts of a baseball game in which each team bats once.
examples: He struck out three batters in the first *inning*.
The game went eleven *innings*.
We left after the seventh *inning*.
contrast: American baseball uses the singular *inning*; British cricket says innings even for one.

gloss: The stroke that puts the ball into play in tennis and similar games.
examples: Her second *serve* went into the net.
He has one of the fastest *serves* on tour.
A good *serve* wins you free points.

gloss: A serve so good the opponent cannot touch it.
examples: He finished the match with eighteen *aces*.
That *ace* saved the set.
She hit an *ace* on match point.

gloss: A baseball at-bat that ends with the batter missing three pitches.
examples: The rookie has more *strikeouts* than anyone.
That *strikeout* ended the inning.
He leads the league in *strikeouts* this season.

gloss: A baseball pitch thrown with spin so that it bends as it drops.
examples: He can't hit a *curveball* to save his life.
The pitcher mixed in two *curveballs*.
Life threw her a *curveball* that spring.

gloss: The number of strokes a good golfer is expected to need for a hole or course.
examples: He finished the round two under *par*.
The seventh hole is a *par* five.
Her score was right at *par*.

gloss: The kick that starts play in football or soccer, or the start of an event.
examples: *Kickoff* is at one o'clock.
He returned the *kickoff* sixty yards.
Both *kickoffs* went out of bounds.
contrast: One word as a noun; the verb is two words: the game *kicks off* at one.

gloss: The act of bringing down or stopping the player with the ball.
examples: That *tackle* knocked the ball loose.
He made eleven *tackles* in the game.
It was a clean *tackle*, not a foul.
contrast: As an uncountable noun *tackle* also means fishing gear: a box of fishing tackle.

gloss: A throw or kick that sends the ball to a teammate.
examples: He threw a perfect *pass* down the sideline.
Three of her *passes* led to goals.
The *pass* was tipped at the line.

gloss: A free shot at the goal from close range, given after a serious foul.
examples: The match was decided by a *penalty kick*.
He has never missed a *penalty kick*.
Both *penalty kicks* went to the same corner.

gloss: Three goals scored by the same player in one game.
examples: She scored a *hat trick* in the semifinal.
That's his second *hat trick* this month.
Fans throw hats on the ice after a *hat trick*.

gloss: The light exercise done before a game or workout.
examples: He pulled a muscle during the *warm-up*.
The *warm-ups* last about fifteen minutes.
Don't skip the *warm-up* in cold weather.
contrast: Hyphenated as a noun; the verb is two words: *warm up* before you run.

gloss: A game or match that a team or player finishes ahead.
examples: That was a big *win* for a young team.
They need three more *wins* to make the playoffs.
It was an ugly *win*, but it counts.

gloss: The competition that decides the best team or player, or the title itself.
examples: They won the state *championship* in overtime.
He has three *championships* in eight years.
The *championship* is played in Dallas this year.

gloss: A game or series played after the regular season to decide a champion.
examples: They lost in the first round of the *playoffs*.
One more win puts them in the *playoff*.
The *playoffs* start the week after Thanksgiving.
contrast: Usually plural in American sports talk: *the playoffs*.

gloss: The round played just before the final.
examples: She lost the *semifinal* in three sets.
Both *semifinals* go on Saturday.
They have never made it past the *semifinal*.

gloss: The table showing how teams rank by wins and losses.
examples: They're in last place in the *standings*.
Check the *standings* before you make a bet.
The *standings* change every night in April.
contrast: Used only in the plural in this sense: *the standings*.

gloss: A player's or team's position on an official list of the best.
examples: Her *ranking* jumped from eleventh to fourth.
The new *rankings* come out on Monday.
He lost his *ranking* after missing a season.

gloss: The extra game or rule used to decide a contest that is level.
examples: The set went to a *tiebreaker*.
Head-to-head record is the first *tiebreaker*.
She has won her last six *tiebreakers*.

gloss: A practice game played against your own team or another one.
examples: They have a *scrimmage* against the JV team Friday.
Nobody gets hurt in these *scrimmages*, usually.
The coach stopped the *scrimmage* to explain the play.

gloss: A session where players compete to be picked for a team.
examples: *Tryouts* are the first week of September.
He made the team after one *tryout*.
She was too nervous at the *tryout*.
contrast: One word as a noun; the verb is two words: *try out* for the team.

gloss: The tight circle a football team forms to call the next play.
examples: The quarterback called the play in the *huddle*.
They ran two plays without a *huddle*.
Both *huddles* broke at the same time.

gloss: A ball dropped by the player carrying it.
examples: His *fumble* cost them the game.
There were four *fumbles* in the rain.
The *fumble* was recovered by the defense.

gloss: A pass caught by the other team.
examples: He threw two *interceptions* in the first half.
That *interception* changed the whole game.
Her *interception* set up the winning score.

gloss: A recovery from being far behind, or a return after time away.
examples: It was the biggest *comeback* in team history.
He's attempting a *comeback* at thirty-eight.
Their *comebacks* are why people watch.

gloss: A surprise win by the side nobody expected to win.
examples: The tournament's biggest *upset* came on day one.
There were three *upsets* in the first round.
Nobody called that game an *upset* afterward.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, UP-set; the verb is up-SET.

gloss: A second match between the same two opponents.
examples: The *rematch* is set for December.
Both *rematches* sold out in an hour.
He wants a *rematch* on his home court.

gloss: A win in boxing when the other fighter cannot get back up.
examples: He won by *knockout* in the third round.
Twenty of her wins were *knockouts*.
That punch was a clean *knockout*.

gloss: A pairing of two teams or players against each other.
examples: It's a tough *matchup* for a young defense.
The *matchups* were announced this morning.
That *matchup* has been building for years.

gloss: The long-running competition between two teams or players.
examples: The *rivalry* goes back to 1902.
College football has the fiercest *rivalries*.
Their *rivalry* sells out every stadium.

gloss: The illegal use of drugs to improve athletic performance.
examples: Two runners were banned for *doping*.
*Doping* controls are done after every race.
The *doping* scandal cost the country its medals.

gloss: The act of putting a fresh player in for one already on the field.
examples: The coach made his last *substitution* in the eightieth minute.
Teams get five *substitutions* now.
That *substitution* changed the game.
contrast: Americans say sub-stih-TOO-shuhn; the British add a y sound: -TYOO-.

gloss: Fair, generous behavior toward opponents in a game.
examples: Shaking hands afterward is basic *sportsmanship*.
The league gives an award for *sportsmanship*.
His *sportsmanship* impressed everyone in the gym.

gloss: The stretch of games played after the regular season ends.
examples: They haven't made the *postseason* since 2015.
He hit better in the *postseason* than in the summer.
Two straight *postseasons* ended in the first round.

gloss: A recording of a play shown again, often to check a call.
examples: The *replay* showed his foot on the line.
They watched three *replays* before reversing the call.
Instant *replay* has changed how games are officiated.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, REE-play; the verb is ree-PLAY.
